nep-prerenal-acute-kidney-injury.title: Prerenal acute kidney injury
nep-prerenal-acute-kidney-injury.summary: Two days of vomiting and poor intake with reduced urine output with dry mucous membranes with a 12-point orthostatic pulse increment is the presentation that defines prerenal acute kidney injury. Urine studies with a fractional excretion of sodium confirms it, and isotonic intravenous volume repletion is the initial management.

sections.heading: Overview
paras: Prerenal acute kidney injury is defined by two days of vomiting and poor intake with reduced urine output, arising from reduced renal perfusion with intact tubular reabsorption. This entry is arranged in the order the problem tends to be encountered: what drives it, how it appears, how it is confirmed, and what is done first.

How often the problem is seen depends on where the counting is done, and case definitions have shifted enough over time that historical series need reading with care. The teaching point most often attached to this topic is that concentrated urine with avid sodium retention is the kidney pleading for volume.

sections.heading: Mechanism
paras: What drives the picture is reduced renal perfusion with intact tubular reabsorption. Its consequences account for both the symptoms the patient reports and the signs found on examination.

Compensatory responses mask the process early and fail late, which is why the interval between the first abnormality and the first symptom can be long. Understanding this is what makes isotonic intravenous volume repletion the rational first response rather than an arbitrary one.

sections.heading: Clinical presentation
paras: Patients most often describe two days of vomiting and poor intake with reduced urine output, and it is the tempo of that history — how quickly it arrived and whether it is progressing — that carries the diagnostic weight.

Partial or atypical presentations are common enough that the absence of one expected feature should not close the question. A history of two days of vomiting and poor intake with reduced urine output in the right context is enough to bring the diagnosis to the front of the differential.

sections.heading: Examination
paras: The sign to look for is dry mucous membranes with a 12-point orthostatic pulse increment; it is more specific than the rest of the examination and is worth eliciting carefully.
Findings are easier to elicit once the process is established, so an unrevealing first examination deserves repeating.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
paras: Evaluation begins with urine studies with a fractional excretion of sodium, which answers the question directly rather than narrowing it by degrees.

A negative result is only as useful as the probability it was applied to, which is the argument for estimating that probability first. The alternative most often confused with it is renal artery stenosis, which is compared below.

nep-autosomal-dominant-polycystic-kidney.title: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
nep-autosomal-dominant-polycystic-kidney.summary: Chronic dull flank fullness with episodic hematuria and a strong family history with bilateral palpable flank masses with elevated blood pressure is the presentation that defines autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. sections.heading: Overview
paras: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease describes the clinical picture of chronic dull flank fullness with episodic hematuria and a strong family history produced by progressive bilateral cyst growth replacing functional parenchyma. Sections below follow one conventional sequence — mechanism, presentation, confirmation, management — and each can be read on its own.

Reported frequency varies with the population studied and with the threshold chosen to define a case, so figures quoted in different sources are rarely directly comparable. The teaching point most often attached to this topic is that blood pressure control is the earliest and most durable intervention available.

sections.heading: Mechanism
paras: The process at work is progressive bilateral cyst growth replacing functional parenchyma. Its consequences account for both the symptoms the patient reports and the signs found on examination.

The rate at which the process develops matters as much as its extent: a gradual change is tolerated where an abrupt one of the same size is not. Understanding this is what makes aggressive blood pressure control with disease-specific referral the rational first response rather than an arbitrary one.

sections.heading: Clinical presentation
paras: The history classically centres on chronic dull flank fullness with episodic hematuria and a strong family history; what refines it is the time course rather than the severity at any one moment.

Presentations at the extremes of age are frequently less typical, and a normal early course does not exclude the diagnosis. A history of chronic dull flank fullness with episodic hematuria and a strong family history in the right context is enough to bring the diagnosis to the front of the differential.

sections.heading: Examination
paras: The sign to look for is bilateral palpable flank masses with elevated blood pressure; it is more specific than the rest of the examination and is worth eliciting carefully.
Findings are easier to elicit once the process is established, so an unrevealing first examination deserves repeating.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
paras: Evaluation begins with abdominal ultrasonography with family-based counseling, which answers the question directly rather than narrowing it by degrees.

nep-pyelonephritis.title: Pyelonephritis
nep-pyelonephritis.summary: Two days of fever, flank pain, and burning urination with costovertebral angle tenderness with a temperature of 38.6°C is the presentation that defines pyelonephritis. Urinalysis with urine culture before antibiotics confirms it, and empiric antibiotic therapy adjusted to culture results is the initial management.

sections.heading: Overview
paras: Pyelonephritis describes the clinical picture of two days of fever, flank pain, and burning urination produced by ascending bacterial infection of the renal parenchyma. This entry is arranged in the order the problem tends to be encountered: what drives it, how it appears, how it is confirmed, and what is done first.

How often the problem is seen depends on where the counting is done, and case definitions have shifted enough over time that historical series need reading with care. The teaching point most often attached to this topic is that culture before the first dose — susceptibility data rescues the failing regimen later.

sections.heading: Mechanism
paras: At the centre of the problem is ascending bacterial infection of the renal parenchyma. Its consequences account for both the symptoms the patient reports and the signs found on examination.

Compensatory responses mask the process early and fail late, which is why the interval between the first abnormality and the first symptom can be long. Understanding this is what makes empiric antibiotic therapy adjusted to culture results the rational first response rather than an arbitrary one.

sections.heading: Clinical presentation
paras: Patients most often describe two days of fever, flank pain, and burning urination, and it is the tempo of that history — how quickly it arrived and whether it is progressing — that carries the diagnostic weight.

Comorbid disease alters the picture, sometimes to the point that the usual pattern is unrecognisable. A history of two days of fever, flank pain, and burning urination in the right context is enough to bring the diagnosis to the front of the differential.

sections.heading: Examination
paras: Costovertebral angle tenderness with a temperature of 38.6°C is the examination finding that most reliably separates this from its closest mimics.
A normal examination early in the course is common and does not argue meaningfully against the diagnosis.

sections.heading: Diagnosis

A negative result is only as useful as the probability it was applied to, which is the argument for estimating that probability first. The alternative most often confused with it is autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, which is compared below.
